title: How three wars are crowding out the challenges that will actually define the next decade
summary: While geopolitical conflicts dominate headlines, the shipping industry's critical decarbonization targets are quietly being missed amidst the distraction. This allows many vessels to continue with excessive HFO usage, maintaining high carbon intensity and delaying vital investments in alternative fuels. Such complacency guarantees future FuelEU Maritime fines and exposes the industry's persistent greenwashing over genuine emissions reduction efforts.
content:
Punit Oza from Maritime NXT on risks that come from crisis distraction, a big topic up for discussion at Thursday’s Splash Singapore conference.

Since early 2026 the world’s attention — and its risk desks, insurance markets, and naval assets — have been consumed by three overlapping conflicts. The Russia-Ukraine war has ground into its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight, Russian drone and missile barrages continuing even as Ukraine’s counter-strikes hit deep into Russian energy infrastructure. The Iran war that erupted in February 2026 has lurched through ceasefire, memorandum, collapse, and resumption, with Hormuz transits still running well below pre-war averages and Brent crude gyrating on every headline out of Islamabad or Tehran. And the Red Sea, which briefly reopened after the Gaza ceasefire, has seen Houthi attacks resume, pushing a meaningful share of Asia-Europe container and tanker traffic back around the Cape of Good Hope.

Each of these crises deserves the attention it gets. Seafarers have died. Cargo has been lost. War-risk premiums have reshaped freight economics overnight. But there is a cost to living permanently in crisis mode: the slower-moving, more consequential shifts reshaping trade, energy, and demography get pushed to the bottom of the agenda — right when decisions taken now will compound for decades.

As I often frame it to my students and clients: a shipowner who only reads the weather report in front of the bow will eventually be surprised by the current underneath the keel. The conflicts are the weather. Climate transition, decarbonization, demographic imbalance, and the reordering of soft power are the current.

Climate change and decarbonisation: quietly missing its own deadline

IMO’s 2023 GHG strategy and the more recent Net-Zero Framework set a trajectory toward net-zero shipping by around mid-century, with interim checkpoints this decade. That trajectory assumed sustained capital flow into alternative fuels, port infrastructure, and fleet renewal. Instead, capital and attention have been diverted toward war-risk cover, convoy escorts, rerouting costs, and bunker price volatility driven by Gulf tensions.

The irony is sharp: every extra week a VLCC spends going around the Cape instead of through the Red Sea burns more fuel and emits more carbon than the direct route — the conflicts are making decarbonization arithmetic harder even as they dominate the news cycle that should be driving decarbonization policy. Green corridors, ammonia and methanol bunkering infrastructure, and newbuild ordering for alternative-fuel tonnage all require long investment horizons and calm capital markets. Geopolitical volatility is the natural enemy of that kind of patient investment.

Demographic imbalance: shipping’s quiet manpower crisis

While headlines track troop movements, a different kind of shortage is building: seafarers. The traditional labour-supplying nations — the Philippines, India, Indonesia, China — face their own demographic transitions, rising domestic wage expectations, and competition from shore-based industries. Meanwhile, officer shortages are already visible in tanker and gas segments, and they will worsen as an aging cohort of experienced masters and chief engineers retires faster than training pipelines can replace them.

This is not a problem conflict created, but conflict has made it worse in a specific way: war-risk transits through the Red Sea and the Gulf have made seafaring measurably more dangerous again, at exactly the moment the industry needs to make the profession more attractive, not less. Crew welfare, hazard pay, and safe-passage guarantees — issues I engage with directly through my work on maritime connectivity and crew welfare technology — deserve as much strategic bandwidth as any war-risk clause, but rarely get it.

China’s soft power: expanding while the West looks elsewhere

Perhaps the most underappreciated shift of the past two years is how much diplomatic and commercial ground China — and to a striking degree, Pakistan as a mediator in the Iran conflict — has covered while Western attention was fixed on Ukraine, Iran, and the Red Sea. Beijing’s involvement was reportedly a factor in nudging Tehran toward the April 2026 ceasefire, a reminder that Chinese leverage in the Gulf now extends well beyond oil purchases into active crisis diplomacy. The Belt and Road Initiative continues to knit together port, rail, and energy infrastructure across the Global South largely without competing Western financing on offer.

For shipping, this matters directly. Port ownership, terminal concessions, and shipbuilding capacity are shifting toward Chinese state and private entities across Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, often as the only credible capital available. Soft power built through infrastructure, financing, and mediation does not show up in a single dramatic headline — it accumulates. By the time it is visible, the map has already changed.

The Asia and Global South pivot: the structural story underneath the noise

Strip away the conflict-driven volatility and a clear structural trend remains: trade gravity continues shifting toward intra-Asia and Global South corridors. Intra-Asian trade volumes, South-South trade flows, and manufacturing relocation out of China into Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, and increasingly parts of Africa are reshaping the map of who ships what, to whom, and through which chokepoints.

Ironically, the very conflicts distracting policymakers are accelerating this pivot. Red Sea disruption has made European buyers reconsider sourcing distance and lead times, favouring nearer, less chokepoint-dependent supply chains. Hormuz volatility has pushed Gulf energy buyers in Asia to diversify sourcing toward the Americas and West Africa. Sanctions on Russian crude have rerouted tanker flows toward India and China at discounted rates, entrenching new trading relationships that will outlast the sanctions themselves. Every disruption is, in effect, redrawing trade lanes in favour of the Global South’s growing consumption base and away from the traditional West-centric axis.

The strategic mindset shipping needs now

None of this argues for ignoring the wars. War risk must be priced, routes must be planned, and crews must be protected — today, not eventually. But the leaders who will be best positioned in 2030 are the ones treating today’s crises and tomorrow’s structural shifts as a single strategic picture, not two separate inboxes.

This is precisely the case for what I call the Chief Geostrategic Officer mindset: maritime and trade leaders cannot simply manage inward-facing operational risk while conflict dominates the horizon. They must simultaneously read the slower currents — decarbonisation deadlines that don’t pause for wars, a workforce that is aging out faster than it is being replenished, a soft-power map being redrawn quietly, and a trade axis tilting decisively toward Asia and the Global South.

The conflicts will eventually settle, as conflicts do. The current underneath will keep moving regardless. The question worth asking in every boardroom and bridge is not only “how do we get through this crisis” but “what did we fail to build while we were looking at it.”
